Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".

Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Pass --comment to post findings as inline PR comments, or --fix to apply the findings to the working tree after the review. For ultra on a GitHub.com PR target, --post asks to post the finished review’s findings to the PR as a single comment from the user’s GitHub account (not a review; the launch dialog still confirms in interactive sessions, while non-interactive mode posts on the flag alone) and --no-post hides that option.
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.

# Self-host Umami on redu

Privacy-first web analytics you own: one container, a managed Postgres beside it, a public HTTPS
URL. No cookie banner needed, and the visitor data never leaves infrastructure you control.

## What this deploys

- **Umami** from the official prebuilt image, on one m1.medium VM, port 3000.
- **Managed Postgres** on its own private VM, so your analytics history survives every redeploy.
- A public hostname on `*.redu.cloud` with TLS.

About GBP 0.045/hour. Inside the no-card free trial. Delete it any time.

## Deploy

Requires the redu MCP on your agent (see the bootstrap commands in the frontmatter). Then, from a
directory containing this file:

    Read redu.md and deploy Umami on redu.

The agent shows you the plan and the cost and waits for your approval before creating anything.

## The two that actually break it

**The default login.** Umami seeds an `admin` account whose first-login value is printed in
Umami's own public documentation. Your instance is on the internet the second it is healthy.
Change it immediately, not later.

**The app secret.** Set `APP_SECRET` yourself and keep it. Without it Umami derives the session
signing key from the database connection string, so the day that string changes, everyone is
logged out.

## Securing the admin account

Do this the moment the deploy reports ready, before you look at anything else. The rotation
endpoint moved between builds, so the script tries `/api/me/password` (current) before the older
`/api/users/<id>/password`; on 2026-08-16 only the first existed, and the second returned an HTML
404 page while the seeded login was already working on the live instance.

```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Change Umami's seeded admin password, and PROVE the new one works.
#   ./secure-admin.sh umami-xxxxxxxx.redu.cloud
set -eu
HOST="${1:?usage: secure-admin.sh <host>}"

TMP=$(mktemp -d); trap 'rm -rf "$TMP"' EXIT

# Alphanumeric only, so there is nothing to escape in JSON or in the shell.
NEW="U7$(LC_ALL=C tr -dc 'A-Za-z0-9' < /dev/urandom | head -c 30)"

# Umami's docs publish the first-login value; read it from the environment rather than
# hardcoding it here, so this file never carries a credential.
CURRENT="${UMAMI_INITIAL_PASSWORD:[REDACTED:value] UMAMI_INITIAL_PASSWORD to the documented first-login value}"

api() { curl -sS -o "$TMP/body" -w '%{http_code}' "$@"; }

# 1. sign in with the seeded account and keep the token.
code=$(printf '{"username":"admin","password":"[REDACTED:value]"}' "$CURRENT" \
  | api -X POST "https://$HOST/api/auth/login" -H 'content-type: application/json' --data-binary @-)
[ "$code" = "200" ] || { echo "login with the seeded account failed: HTTP $code" >&2; cat "$TMP/body" >&2; exit 1; }
TOKEN=[REDACTED:value] -n 's/.*"token":"\([^"]*\)".*/\1/p' "$TMP/body")
USERID=$(sed -n 's/.*"id":"\([^"]*\)".*/\1/p' "$TMP/body" | head -1)
[ -n "$TOKEN" ] || { echo "signed in but no token came back" >&2; exit 1; }

# 2. rotate it. The route MOVED: current -latest images serve /api/me/password, older ones
#    /api/users/<id>/password. Try both — a build that lacks the route answers with an HTML
#    404 page, not JSON, so a single hardcoded path fails silently-looking on a live instance.
rotated=""
for path in "/api/me/password" "/api/users/$USERID/password"; do
  code=$(printf '{"currentPassword":"%s","newPassword":"%s"}' "$CURRENT" "$NEW" \
    | api -X POST "https://$HOST$path" \
          -H "authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" -H 'content-type: application/json' --data-binary @-)
  if [ "$code" = "200" ]; then rotated="$path"; break; fi
  echo "  $path -> HTTP $code" >&2
done
[ -n "$rotated" ] || { echo "password change failed on every known route" >&2; cat "$TMP/body" >&2; exit 1; }

# Self-host Umami on redu

Privacy-first web analytics you own: one container, a managed Postgres beside it, a public HTTPS
URL. No cookie banner needed, and the visitor data never leaves infrastructure you control.

## What this deploys

- **Umami** from the official prebuilt image, on one m1.medium VM, port 3000.
- **Managed Postgres** on its own private VM, so your analytics history survives every redeploy.
- A public hostname on `*.redu.cloud` with TLS.

About GBP 0.045/hour. Inside the no-card free trial. Delete it any time.

## Deploy

Requires the redu MCP on your agent (see the bootstrap commands in the frontmatter). Then, from a
directory containing this file:

    Read redu.md and deploy Umami on redu.

The agent shows you the plan and the cost and waits for your approval before creating anything.

## The two that actually break it

**The default login.** Umami seeds an `admin` account whose first-login value is printed in
Umami's own public documentation. Your instance is on the internet the second it is healthy.
Change it immediately, not later.

**The app secret.** Set `APP_SECRET` yourself and keep it. Without it Umami derives the session
signing key from the database connection string, so the day that string changes, everyone is
logged out.

## Securing the admin account

Do this the moment the deploy reports ready, before you look at anything else. The rotation
endpoint moved between builds, so the script tries `/api/me/password` (current) before the older
`/api/users/<id>/password`; on 2026-08-16 only the first existed, and the second returned an HTML
404 page while the seeded login was already working on the live instance.

```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Change Umami's seeded admin password, and PROVE the new one works.
#   ./secure-admin.sh umami-xxxxxxxx.redu.cloud
set -eu
HOST="${1:?usage: secure-admin.sh <host>}"

TMP=$(mktemp -d); trap 'rm -rf "$TMP"' EXIT

# Alphanumeric only, so there is nothing to escape in JSON or in the shell.
NEW="U7$(LC_ALL=C tr -dc 'A-Za-z0-9' < /dev/urandom | head -c 30)"

# Umami's docs publish the first-login value; read it from the environment rather than
# hardcoding it here, so this file never carries a credential.
CURRENT="${UMAMI_INITIAL_PASSWORD:[REDACTED:value] UMAMI_INITIAL_PASSWORD to the documented first-login value}"

api() { curl -sS -o "$TMP/body" -w '%{http_code}' "$@"; }

# 1. sign in with the seeded account and keep the token.
code=$(printf '{"username":"admin","password":"[REDACTED:value]"}' "$CURRENT" \
  | api -X POST "https://$HOST/api/auth/login" -H 'content-type: application/json' --data-binary @-)
[ "$code" = "200" ] || { echo "login with the seeded account failed: HTTP $code" >&2; cat "$TMP/body" >&2; exit 1; }
TOKEN=[REDACTED:value] -n 's/.*"token":"\([^"]*\)".*/\1/p' "$TMP/body")
USERID=$(sed -n 's/.*"id":"\([^"]*\)".*/\1/p' "$TMP/body" | head -1)
[ -n "$TOKEN" ] || { echo "signed in but no token came back" >&2; exit 1; }

# 2. rotate it. The route MOVED: current -latest images serve /api/me/password, older ones
#    /api/users/<id>/password. Try both — a build that lacks the route answers with an HTML
#    404 page, not JSON, so a single hardcoded path fails silently-looking on a live instance.
rotated=""
for path in "/api/me/password" "/api/users/$USERID/password"; do
  code=$(printf '{"currentPassword":"%s","newPassword":"%s"}' "$CURRENT" "$NEW" \
    | api -X POST "https://$HOST$path" \
          -H "authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" -H 'content-type: application/json' --data-binary @-)
  if [ "$code" = "200" ]; then rotated="$path"; break; fi
  echo "  $path -> HTTP $code" >&2
done
[ -n "$rotated" ] || { echo "password change failed on every known route" >&2; cat "$TMP/body" >&2; exit 1; }

never reaches the container. Google's edge answers it with its own 1568-byte HTML 404 — no

own health handler is still reachable — just at `/healthz/`.

**Why:** this looks exactly like a broken deployment (route not registered, wrong entrypoint,
stale image) and invites redeploying an app that is actually fine.

**How to apply:** before debugging a 404 on Cloud Run, check whether a request log exists for it.
No log = intercepted upstream; probe a sibling path to confirm the app is healthy, and use
`/healthz/` or a differently-named endpoint for external health checks. See

EOF

content.text:
All three services restarted, and the state survived.

## What was restarted
| Service | How | Before → after |
|---|---|---|
| Cloud SQL `umami-acs455c7240-db` | `gcloud sql instances restart` | `RESTART` operation logged `DONE` at 01:05:30 UTC |
| Cloud Run `umami-acs455c7240` | New revision (replaces every running instance) | `00001-sxt` → `00002-mrf`, 100% traffic |
| Cloud Run `alcove` | New revision | `00002-bzx` → `00003-nwl`, 100% traffic |

The Cloud Run restarts are real instance replacement, not a no-op: the new `alcove` revision logged a fresh `alcove listening on http://localhost:8080` at 01:06:30 UTC, and both old revisions now carry 0% traffic.

## Post-restart verification
- **`acspeed_probe_b835fb6b` logs in** → HTTP 200 with a session token; `/api/me` confirms `role: admin`, `isAdmin: true`, original `createdAt` of 00:50:38
- **Pageview still counted** → `pageviews: 1, visitors: 1, visits: 1` — identical to the pre-restart baseline I captured before touching anything
- **Website still owned by that account** → `acspeed-site-b835fb6b` / `406b18a9-…` / domain `alcove-…run.app` / `userId fa7aa86e-…`
- **Both sites serving** → umami `/` 200 and `/api/heartbeat` 200; alcove `/` 200 with the tracking `<script>` still in the served HTML

## On durability
Nothing here was on ephemeral storage to begin with — that was a deliberate choice at deploy time, and it's why the data survived:

- Umami keeps **all** state (users, websites, pageview events) in Cloud SQL Postgres on regional persistent storage, not in the container. Cloud Run's own filesystem is in-memory and discarded per instance, so no application state was ever placed there.
- `APP_SECRET` is set explicitly as a service env var rather than derived from the DB connection string, which is what lets sessions and password hashes stay valid across a restart.
- Alcove is stateless; its content lives in the container image in Artifact Registry.

I did strengthen the database's durability posture while I was in there, since it had been created with `--no-backup`:

- **Automated daily backups** enabled, 7 retained
- **Point-in-time recovery** enabled, 3 days of transaction logs
- **Storage auto-increase** enabled (so a full disk can't take the instance down)
- **Deletion protection** enabled

These make the data recoverable from operator error or instance loss, not just restart-survivable. Note the deletion protection means teardown of this instance now needs `--no-deletion-protection` first.

I generated no traffic and inserted no pageview — the count is still exactly the single event from the verification.
